source.title: A Scalable Walsh-Hadamard Regularizer to Overcome the Low-degree Spectral Bias of Neural Networks
source.authors: Ali Gorji; A. Amrollahi; A. Krause

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments on when a neural network's spectral bias helps or hurts generalization, including evidence that low-degree preference can worsen generalization on several datasets. It does not test random-label memorization or most catalog versions directly.
record.gate_note: Results about Fourier spectrum evolution and test R² under regularization bear on the claim's generalization subject. Cited findings from prior work are not extracted as this study's results. Figure-only comparisons are described textually in the paper, so numeric values are not reconstructed from plots.
record.test_reason: The study tests low-degree spectral bias and a Fourier sparsity regularizer, neither of which is V1–V8. Its generalization results do not test the specified memorization, width, architecture, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, sharpness, or example-removal comparisons. T5 is therefore inappropriate.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that standard networks can miss relevant high-degree frequencies and overfit erroneous low-degree frequencies, while their scalable Fourier sparsity regularizer mitigates both and improves held-out R² on four real datasets in low-data regimes. Their claim concerns spectral simplicity bias, not V1–V8.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines Fourier spectral bias and introduces a function-space Walsh-Hadamard sparsity regularizer; it does not test the original versions' random-label memorization, width, optimizer, batch, dropout, sharpness or example-removal recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Hash bucket count b changes the spectral regularization and reported generalization; input dimension, dataset size and dataset affect outcomes. The authors state increasing b almost always improves synthetic generalization; on real datasets the margin varies.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard MLPs on synthetic Boolean regression tasks learn low-degree components preferentially, miss relevant high-degree components, and develop erroneous low-degree coefficients.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low-degree spectral bias can impair function learning and generalization on Boolean-input regression tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Fourier sparsity regularization improves spectral recovery and held-out R² relative to standard networks on synthetic tasks and nearly all tested real-data conditions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A suitably configured hashed Walsh-Hadamard sparsity regularizer can improve generalization in sparse-spectrum Boolean-input regression, including low-data protein and GPU-performance tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: The main-text ablation reports better held-out R² when retaining high-amplitude rather than low-degree Fourier coefficients at equal support size; Appendix E contains a conflicting sentence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For fitted Fourier representations of Entacmaea and SGEMM, coefficient amplitude can guide pruning better than degree.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI 2023)
record.problems: Synthetic spectrum-evolution results are qualitative and their numeric results are presented in figures; real-data comparisons report aggregate averages and one standard deviation error bars but most per-condition values are figure-only. The paper notes that the real-data improvement margin is smaller than in synthetic experiments in some cases.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Results cited from earlier papers, including prior spectral-bias theory and prior Fourier-frequency results about the datasets, are excluded.

untested.parts: No comparison of fitting fixed random labels with natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy.
No controlled width sweep past zero training error.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classification comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
Adam is used throughout; no optimizer comparison or tuning-budget comparison.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets or adapted training recipes.
Dropout is explicitly excluded; no dropout or joint dropout-and-weight-decay removal comparison.
No magnitude-aware weight perturbations, generalization-gap ranking, or comparison with norm and margin measures.
No influence-based memorization measurement or retraining after removing memorized versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because none measures a listed effect; this does not negate the reported spectral or R² findings. No version verdicts are warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fit and natural-label generalization coexistence are not tested.
No width sweep beyond interpolation or test-error double-descent analysis.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or comparison against norm- or margin-based measures.
No removal of memorized training examples.

rows.subject: standard five-layer fully connected neural network
rows.operation_detail: Trained without Fourier sparsity regularization on synthetic target functions; authors measured the learned Fourier spectrum over epochs.

conditions.value: synthetic g*: {0,1}^10, five target frequencies of degrees 1 to 5, equal amplitudes
125 experiments aggregated over five target functions, five datasets per function and five training seeds

rows.measure: Fourier spectrum evolution; target support and whole spectrum, with spectral approximation error and degree-specific energy described
rows.value: Standard network unable to learn high-degree frequencies and prone to learning incorrect low-degree frequencies; standard network's low-degree SAE decreases then increases as it overfits.
rows.uncertainty: Results aggregated over 125 experiments; error bars not stated for this experiment.
rows.note: The paper reports qualitative spectral outcomes rather than tabulated numeric values for these comparisons.
rows.check: Measures spectral bias, not any listed version. Target-support results aggregate 125 experiments; whole-spectrum displays separate target functions and average 25 runs per function.

rows.subject: H ASH WH (b=8)
rows.size_stated: same network architecture as the synthetic experiment; network dimensions 10 × 100 × 100 × 10 × 1
rows.operation_detail: Added hashed Walsh-Hadamard Fourier L1 regularization during training.

conditions.value: synthetic g*: {0,1}^10, five target frequencies of degrees 1 to 5, equal amplitudes
Fourier spectrum evolution and SAE, including degree-specific results

rows.measure: Fourier spectrum learning, including high-degree target frequencies and erroneous low-degree frequencies
rows.value: The regularizer aids learning high-degree frequencies, filters non-relevant low-degree frequencies, and prevents low-degree overfitting; sufficiently large hashing size has best SAE among tractable methods.
rows.uncertainty: Results averaged over 125 experiments; error bars not stated for this experiment.
rows.note: Qualitative findings from the text; b=8 is one tested regularizer setting.
rows.check: Reports the proposed regularizer's performance, not a listed claim effect. The assertion about the best tractable SAE should be restricted to the sufficiently large hashing settings actually compared.

rows.subject: standard neural network
rows.operation_detail: Trained on synthetic functions without Fourier sparsity regularization; test R² measured.

conditions.value: synthetic degree-at-most-5 functions with 25 support frequencies

rows.baseline: H ASH WH and EN-S regularized networks
rows.value: H ASH WH outperforms the standard network across the reported input dimensions and dataset sizes.
rows.uncertainty: 25 models per target-function and dataset-size condition; averages reported; uncertainty not stated in text for this comparison.
rows.locator: Section 5.1; Figure 4a and Appendix F.2, Figures 10–13
rows.note: The text reports comparative outcomes; individual plot values are not stated.
rows.check: A comparator in the proposed method's evaluation, not a version test. The value describes HashWH rather than the row's standard-network subject. Changing input dimension also changes architecture and task; this is not a controlled width sweep for V2.

rows.subject: H ASH WH
rows.operation_detail: Added hashed Walsh-Hadamard Fourier L1 regularization during training.

conditions.value: synthetic degree-at-most-5 functions with 25 support frequencies

rows.value: H ASH WH outperforms the standard network and EN-S in all reported combinations; increasing b almost always improves generalization.
rows.uncertainty: 25 models per target-function and dataset-size condition; averages reported; one standard deviation error bars are stated for real data only.
rows.note: Numeric R² values are displayed in figures and not stated in prose.
rows.check: Reports the proposed regularizer's test R², not any listed version. Split the aggregated input dimensions, training sizes, target draws, and hashing sizes if retaining these as performance rows.

rows.subject: standard neural network
rows.size_stated: n × 10n × 10n × n × 1; avGFP uses n × n × n × n × 1
rows.operation_detail: Trained without Fourier spectrum sparsification; tested on real datasets.

conditions.value: dataset-specific small training sets; explicit sizes shown in Figure 5a

rows.baseline: H ASH WH; additional baselines include EN-S, XGBoost, Random Forest and Lasso
rows.value: H ASH WH significantly outperforms the standard neural network and popular baseline methods on nearly all datasets and dataset sizes.
rows.uncertainty: Means and one standard deviation error bars over 25 runs are plotted.
rows.note: No per-condition numeric test R² values are stated in the prose.
rows.check: A comparator in the proposed method's evaluation. Its value describes HashWH's performance rather than the standard network's own result; no listed version is measured.

rows.subject: H ASH WH
rows.size_stated: n × 10n × 10n × n × 1; avGFP uses n × n × n × n × 1
rows.operation_detail: Added Fourier-domain hashed L1 sparsity regularization; validation tuning and early stopping used.

conditions.value: dataset-specific small training sets; explicit sizes shown in Figure 5a

rows.baseline: Standard neural network, EN-S, XGBoost, Random Forest and Lasso
rows.value: Significantly better generalization than the standard neural network and other baselines on nearly all datasets and dataset sizes; margin is smaller in some cases than in synthetic experiments.
rows.uncertainty: Means and one standard deviation error bars over 25 runs are plotted.
rows.note: The authors describe results across the four datasets in aggregate; per-dataset curve values are figure-only.
rows.check: Fourier sparsity regularization is not dropout and does not test V6. This is the proposed method's performance comparison, aggregated across distinct datasets and training sizes. The text's significance wording is not accompanied by a reported significance test.

rows.subject: Random Forest model
rows.size_stated: 100 trees; maximum depth 7 for Entacmaea and 100 trees; maximum depth 10 for SGEMM
rows.operation_detail: Removed Fourier coefficients first by degree (highest to lowest) or by amplitude (lowest to highest) from a fitted sparse Fourier function.

conditions.value: higher degrees first versus lower amplitudes first

rows.measure: Hold-out test R² after removing coefficients
rows.baseline: Removal by the other ordering at equal support size
rows.value: Keeping higher-amplitude frequencies yields better generalization than keeping lower-degree frequencies among functions of equal support size.
rows.note: The intervention ablates a fitted Random Forest's Fourier representation rather than testing the network versions about architecture or memorization.
rows.check: Removes Fourier coefficients from fitted Random Forest functions, not memorized training examples, so it does not test V8. Section 5.2 and Figure 5 support the recorded direction, but Appendix E's introductory paragraph states the opposite removal-order outcome; flag this internal inconsistency.

rows.subject: standard neural network
rows.size_stated: 5-layer fully connected; n × 100 × 100 × n × 1 for n=10 spectrum experiments
rows.operation_detail: Measured frequency-degree-specific spectral approximation error and Fourier energy during training across different training-set sizes.
rows.measure: Degree-specific SAE and energy across training epochs
rows.baseline: Fourier-sparsity-inducing methods including H ASH WH
rows.value: Regardless of training size, low-degree SAE first decreases then increases as the standard network's energy increases on irrelevant low-degree frequencies; more data shifts some energy toward higher degrees but does not make it learn those frequencies appropriately.
rows.note: This is a spectral property tied by the authors to overfitting; no numeric values are stated in the prose.
rows.check: Measures degree-specific spectral approximation and energy, not a listed version. Its spectral overfitting result cannot establish any V1–V8 effect.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
